newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Air Afrique deb solution hits new snag.
newsitem.headline: Air Afrique deb solution hits new snag.

text.p: Attempts by Air Afrique to find a solution to its crippling debt problem have hit a fresh snag with a demand by one potential saviour for interest payments on money it has agreed to pay into a new leasing company.
Ministers from the 11 francophone African states that own the airline met in Abidjan on June 3 and 4.

According to the minutes, francophone Africa air safety agency ASECNA, which had agreed to put some of its surplus funds into a new leasing company to take over Air Afrique's planes and its debt, now wanted interest on its investment.
"It has been noted that ASECNA is now making its participation in the capital dependent on the payment of three percent interest on the sums it commits," the minutes said.
The minutes said that "this problem will be debated at the next ASECNA meeting in Madagascar", scheduled for June 23.
The recovery plan has also been hampered by the fact that, of the 11 member states, only Ivory Coast and Senegal have paid their one billion CFA francs contribution to the new company.

Air Afrique has debts of some 200 billion CFA francs ($350 million) and was supposed to have paid off 31 billion CFA francs in arrears by the end of last year. A deadline of March 31 set by creditors has also passed without progress being made.
It appointed a new managing director, Sir Harry Tirvengadum, formerly head of Air Mauritius, at the start of the year, after the member states effectively sacked predecessor Yves-Rolland Billecart.
Much of the debt was contracted to buy planes in the early 1990s, but the company hit serious repayment problems after the 50 percent devaluation of the CFA franc in 1994.

A large part of its revenue is denominated in CFA francs, the common currency of 15 African states in the Franc Zone, including all but one of Air Afrique's member states. The debt was denominated in dollars.
The minutes of the meeting also show the ministers striving for more cooperation between the national carriers of the member states on the one hand and Air Afrique on the other.
A new article in the company's statutes now obliges each shareholding state to give Air Afrique priority traffic rights on the international routes it covers.
A country may still retain the right for its national carrier to serve neighbouring countries and some other routes traditionally covered by Air Afrique.

But, the minutes stress: "In these cases, the state will take the necessary steps to ensure that this is done in coordination with Air Afrique, out of a concern to be complementary rather than in competition."

In addition to Ivory Coast and Senegal, the states that own Air Afrique are Benin, Burkina Faso, Central African Republic, Congo, Mali, Mauritania, Niger, Chad and Togo. Air France also has a small stake. ($ = 580 CFA francs)
